common_name: Carla Black's Anthurium (Velvet Bird's Nest Anthurium)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix of orchid bark, perlite, and sphagnum; this self-heading species forms a tight rosette rather than climbing.

directions: Anthurium carlablackiae is a recently described terrestrial aroid from the Panama-Colombia border region, growing low in deep leaf litter and building a compact, self-heading crown of tightly stacked internodes rather than climbing or trailing. The broad, heart-shaped leaves are deep velvety near-black green overlaid with crisp, contrasting white venation, and the petioles darken to burgundy with age, giving the whole plant an unusually dramatic two-tone appearance. Keep humidity high and use a very open, fast-draining substrate, since the species is naturally accustomed to loose, well-aerated leaf litter rather than dense potting soil. Protect from temperatures below 60 degrees Fahrenheit and from direct sun, which will scorch the velvety foliage.

planting.note: Grow mounted on bark or in a chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix in bright, indirect light; leaf division into finger-like lobes increases dramatically as the plant matures from its juvenile form.

directions: Anthurium podophyllum is an epiphytic aroid native to cloud forests of coastal Veracruz and Oaxaca, Mexico, where it clings to tree trunks at higher elevations. Juvenile leaves are simple and undivided, but mature foliage splits palmately into three or more elongated, almost free-standing lobes radiating from the leaf base, a striking transformation that gives the species its podophyllum ("foot-leaf") epithet. Grow in a very open bark-based mix with excellent airflow around the roots, since the plant is accustomed to mounting on trunks rather than sitting in dense soil. Keep consistently humid and out of direct sun, and expect the plant's leaf shape to change noticeably as it ages, so do not judge a young specimen's mature form too early.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix in bright, indirect light with a small support for its creeping-to-climbing habit; high humidity keeps the narrow lobes from browning at the tips.

directions: Anthurium polyschistum is a slender, creeping to climbing aroid native to the Andean foothills of Colombia, Ecuador, and northeastern Bolivia, grown for its unmistakable, deeply divided foliage. Each leaf splits into five to nine or more narrow, elongated, wavy-margined lobes radiating outward like fingers from a central point, creating a spidery silhouette very different from the broad, solid leaves of most other collector anthuriums. Provide semi-shade, evenly moist but well-drained media, and a small totem or piece of bark for the stems to grip as the plant matures. Its slighter, more delicate growth habit compared to the larger velvet-leaf anthuriums makes it well suited to terrariums, cabinets, or smaller shaded display spaces.

common_name: Green Congo Philodendron (Congo Green Self-Heading Philodendron)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio specimen in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; this self-heading hybrid needs no climbing support and forms a dense clump on its own.

directions: Philodendron 'Congo Green' is a bred, self-heading hybrid within the erubescens complex, developed for its bold, low-maintenance rosette habit rather than climbing growth. Large, glossy, broadly ovate to elliptical leaves emerge from a compact central stem, maturing from bright to deep emerald green and reaching 10 to 18 inches long on established plants. Because it never sends out long climbing vines, it holds a tidy, symmetrical shape without staking or pruning, making it a popular structural accent for shaded interiorscapes, lobbies, and covered patios. It shares its parentage and general culture with the darker-leaved 'Rojo Congo', but 'Congo Green' keeps its foliage a uniform rich green rather than developing burgundy tones.

planting.note: Give a sturdy pole or trunk to climb in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; young plants shingle flat against the support before producing large mature leaves.

directions: Monstera punctulata is a robust climbing aroid native to southern Mexico and Central America, capable of scaling large rainforest trees to 50 feet or more in the wild. Juvenile plants go through a shingling phase, pressing flattened stems and leaves tightly against their support, and the petioles are often densely flecked with small white spots that give the species its punctulata ("little dots") name. Mature leaves are soft-textured, matte rather than glossy, and grow quite large on well-established specimens climbing a tall moss pole or bark slab. Keep the growing medium evenly moist, provide consistently warm and humid conditions, and expect a slow transition from the compact juvenile shingling stage to larger adult foliage over several years.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light in a well-drained potting mix with a small trellis or moss pole for support as the vine matures; variegation is brightest under stronger indirect light.

directions: Syngonium podophyllum 'Three Kings' is a variegated arrowhead-plant cultivar named for the three distinct shades of green and cream typically visible on each leaf, ranging from pale minty tones to yellow-green and deep forest green in irregular, unpredictable patterns. Sold previously in the trade under the name 'Jade', it is a vigorous climbing vine that starts with simple arrowhead-shaped juvenile leaves and develops larger, more deeply lobed foliage as it matures and is given a support to climb. Bright indirect light is important for keeping the pale variegated sectors from reverting to solid green. Like other Syngonium, all parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic to pets and people if ingested.
sources: Little Prince of Oregon Nursery listing

planting.note: Grow in bright to medium indirect light in a well-drained potting mix, training the vine onto a moss pole or trellis so the mature three-lobed leaves have room to develop fully.

directions: Syngonium podophyllum 'Trileaf Wonder' is a classic solid deep-green cultivar prized for the way its foliage transforms with age: juvenile growth shows the typical simple arrowhead shape, but mature leaves under good climbing conditions split into three distinct, elliptic, pointed lobes, and occasionally more on well-established vines. This vigorous climber is unusually adaptable to average household humidity and a wide range of indoor light levels compared to more delicate variegated Syngonium cultivars. Provide a support for the aerial roots to grip as the plant grows, since the more dramatic lobed leaf form only develops fully once the vine is climbing rather than trailing. All parts are toxic if ingested by pets or people.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light in a well-drained potting mix; the delicate vein-following variegation pattern is best preserved with steady moderate-to-high humidity and no harsh direct sun.

directions: Syngonium podophyllum 'Batik', also sold as 'Golden Venation', is named for the way its pale cream to light-green variegation follows the leaf's vein network in a fine, orderly lattice rather than forming the random blotchy sectors seen in cultivars like 'Albo' or 'Three Kings'. The resulting lace-like pattern gives each arrowhead-shaped leaf a distinct, almost hand-drawn appearance that intensifies with brighter indirect light. It grows as a climbing to trailing vine and benefits from a small support once it starts to lengthen, though it also performs well cascading from a hanging basket or shelf. Keep the soil evenly moist but not waterlogged, and remember all Syngonium tissue contains calcium oxalate crystals that are toxic if chewed or ingested.

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light in a well-drained aroid mix with a moss pole for climbing support; turn a leaf over occasionally to enjoy the burgundy undersides that give this species its name.

directions: Syngonium erythrophyllum, commonly called Red Arrow, is native to the rainforests of Panama and Colombia and is grown for the striking contrast between its dark green, velvety-textured, arrow-shaped upper leaf surfaces and their rich burgundy-red undersides. As the plant matures and begins climbing, the simple arrowhead leaves gradually give way to a more lobed shape, following the same juvenile-to-adult leaf transformation seen in other Syngonium species. It climbs readily on a moss pole or bark slab in cultivation, clinging with aerial roots, and prefers consistently warm, humid conditions similar to its native forest floor and lower-canopy habitat. All plant parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested by pets or people.

planting.note: Grow in mostly shade to partial shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil with a support for climbing; this species keeps its broad, unsegmented leaf shape at maturity rather than splitting into lobes.

directions: Syngonium macrophyllum is a vigorous climbing aroid distinguished from most cultivated Syngonium by leaves that stay broad, hastate, and unsegmented even at full size, rather than dividing into multiple lobes as the plant ages. The thick, semi-matte leaf blades can grow more than two feet long on well-established vines, with light blue-green petioles often carrying a fine, powdery white coating. It grows well in mostly shaded conditions with consistently moist, well-drained soil, and climbs readily once given a mossy pole or similar rough support for its aerial roots to grip. Its coarser texture and larger, simpler leaves make it a good textural contrast to the smaller, more finely lobed Syngonium species and cultivars.

planting.note: Divide clumps or plant nursery starts in spring in a rich, well-drained potting mix in partial shade; brighter indirect light intensifies the red-and-gold leaf coloration without risking direct-sun scorch.

directions: Aglaonema 'Red Gold' is a hybrid Chinese evergreen selected for its heavily variegated foliage, which combines glossy green leaf centers with irregular streaks of red and yellow and distinct red leaf margins. Like other Aglaonema, it tolerates the low light, dry indoor air, and inconsistent watering that make this genus one of the most durable interior foliage plants available, though the red-gold coloration develops most vividly in bright, indirect light rather than deep shade. The clumping, cane-forming habit stays compact enough for tabletop or floor display and slowly widens over time through basal offsets, which can be divided to propagate new plants. Keep away from temperatures below 55 degrees Fahrenheit and out of direct sun, which can bleach the colorful variegation.

planting.note: Divide clumps or plant nursery starts in spring in a rich, well-drained potting mix in partial to deep shade; this compact, bushy cultivar tolerates lower indoor light better than most flowering houseplants.

directions: Aglaonema commutatum 'King of Siam' bears large, elliptical to oval leaves patterned in dark green, silver, and touches of red, giving it a richer and more varied coloration than the plainer species form. The compact, bushy clump habit stays tidy without pruning and slowly spreads by basal offsets that can be divided for propagation. As with most Aglaonema, it is valued for tolerating the low light and inconsistent watering typical of interior spaces far better than most other flowering foliage plants, making it a dependable choice for offices and rooms without strong natural light. Protect from temperatures below 55 degrees Fahrenheit and avoid direct sun, which fades the leaf variegation.

planting.note: Divide clumps or plant nursery starts in spring in a rich, well-drained potting mix in deep to partial shade; this large-leaved selection tolerates lower light than almost any other houseplant of comparable size.

directions: Aglaonema nitidum 'Curtisii' produces some of the largest leaves in the genus, glossy jade-green and up to 18 inches long, with silvery-gray variegation tracing the lateral veins in an irregular feathered pattern. Named for nineteenth-century plant collector Charles Curtis, who gathered the wild form in the forests of peninsular Malaysia, this cultivar has also been an important parent in breeding other well-known Aglaonema hybrids. Its tolerance for low light makes it especially useful in offices and interior rooms where few other large-leaved foliage plants perform well. Keep evenly moist but not waterlogged, protect from temperatures below 55 degrees Fahrenheit, and avoid direct sun, which will scorch the broad leaves.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide clumps or plant nursery starts in spring in a rich, well-drained potting mix in bright but filtered shade; this species needs warmer, more humid conditions than common mass-market Chinese evergreens.

directions: Aglaonema rotundum is endemic to the rainforests of North Sumatra and stands out among Chinese evergreens as one of the few species with genuinely red leaf coloration rather than the more typical green-and-silver patterning. The rounded, velvety leaves are dark green above with vivid pink-to-red veins and a contrasting reddish underside, producing one of the strongest color contrasts found in any true-species Aglaonema. It stays smaller and more compact than the common commutatum-type Chinese evergreens sold in mass-market nurseries, making it well suited to shelves or small plant stands. Because of its Sumatran rainforest origin, it prefers warmer temperatures, brighter filtered light, and higher humidity than typical big-box Aglaonema and resents cold drafts or dry indoor air.
